questions.question: What is a Merkle tree?

options.text: A hash tree where each leaf is a hash of data and each non-leaf is a hash of its children

questions.explanation: Merkle tree: leaves contain hashes of data blocks, parent nodes contain hashes of children. Root hash represents entire dataset. Enables efficient verification—changing any data changes the root hash.

questions.question: How do Merkle trees help in distributed systems?

options.text: They enable efficient comparison and synchronization of large datasets

questions.explanation: Merkle trees enable efficient sync: compare root hashes to detect differences, then traverse tree to find exactly which data differs. Used in databases (Cassandra anti-entropy), blockchain, and file sync (Git).

questions.question: What is HyperLogLog?

options.text: A probabilistic data structure for estimating cardinality (count of unique elements)

questions.explanation: HyperLogLog estimates unique element count using minimal memory (~12KB for billions of elements). Probabilistic—has small error (~0.81%). Used for counting unique visitors, distinct values at scale.

questions.question: When would you use HyperLogLog instead of exact counting?

options.text: When counting unique elements at massive scale where small error is acceptable

questions.explanation: HyperLogLog for massive scale: counting unique visitors across billions of events, distinct IPs, unique search queries. Exact counting would require storing all values (huge memory). HLL trades accuracy for efficiency.

questions.question: What is a Geohash?

options.text: A system that encodes geographic coordinates into a short string, enabling proximity searches

questions.explanation: Geohash encodes latitude/longitude into a string (e.g., 'u4pruydqqvj'). Nearby locations share prefixes. Enables efficient proximity queries: find all locations starting with 'u4pru'. Used in location-based services.

questions.question: What is a Quadtree?

options.text: A tree that recursively divides 2D space into four quadrants for spatial indexing

questions.explanation: Quadtree divides 2D space into four quadrants recursively. Each node has four children. Efficient for spatial queries: finding points in a region, nearest neighbor. Used in maps, games, image processing.

questions.question: What is a Skip List?

options.text: A probabilistic data structure with multiple levels of linked lists for O(log n) search

questions.explanation: Skip list: multiple levels of linked lists. Higher levels skip more elements, enabling binary search-like O(log n) operations. Simpler than balanced trees. Used in Redis sorted sets, LevelDB.

questions.question: What is Count-Min Sketch?

options.text: A probabilistic data structure for estimating frequency of elements in a stream

questions.explanation: Count-Min Sketch estimates how often elements appear in a data stream using sub-linear space. May overestimate (never underestimate). Used for: heavy hitters detection, frequency estimation at scale.

questions.question: True or False: Bloom filters can tell you exactly which elements are in a set.
questions.explanation: Bloom filters only answer membership queries (is X in set?), not enumeration. They can't list elements. Also, they have false positives—'probably yes' or 'definitely no'. Trade-off for space efficiency.

questions.question: Which data structures are probabilistic? (Choose all that apply)
questions.explanation: Probabilistic structures trade accuracy for space/time: Bloom filter (membership), HyperLogLog (cardinality), Count-Min Sketch (frequency). B-tree is deterministic—exact results, more space.

questions.question: What problem does consistent hashing with virtual nodes solve?

options.text: Uneven data distribution when nodes have different capacities

questions.explanation: Virtual nodes: each physical node has multiple positions on the hash ring. More virtual nodes = more data. Enables: proportional distribution based on capacity, smoother rebalancing when nodes change.

questions.question: A system needs to find the top 100 most frequent items in a stream of billions of events. Which approach is most practical?

options.text: Use Count-Min Sketch with a heap for top-k tracking

questions.explanation: Count-Min Sketch estimates frequencies in constant space. Combined with a min-heap tracking top-k, efficiently finds heavy hitters. Storing all events is impractical at billions scale. Sampling might miss important items.
